chunks: "Current gain, or beta, is the ratio of collector current to base current in the forward-active region: beta equals I C over I B .
For a small-signal transistor it's typically 50 to 300, so a base current of 10 microamps controls a collector current of about 1 to 3 milliamps.
The related quantity alpha is the collector current over the emitter current, which is just under one, and the two are linked: beta equals alpha over (1- alpha) . If alpha is 0.

It comes from the physics: of all the carriers the emitter injects, almost all reach the collector, and only a small fraction is lost to recombination in the thin base or to holes injected back into the emitter.
The base current replaces those losses. A thinner base and a more heavily doped emitter give higher beta.
The key engineering point is that beta isn't a precise or constant number.
It varies from part to part by a factor of two or three, it changes with collector current, with V CE , and with temperature, rising when hot and dropping when cold.
So I never design a circuit that depends on a particular beta.
For an amplifier I use emitter degeneration and a stiff base-bias divider so I C is set by resistors and not by beta.
For a switch I use a forced beta of about 10, so it saturates even on the lowest-gain parts."
